strengths: The manuscript studies an important problem: obtaining flexible conditional-independence tests that retain operator-based generality while improving the scalability of kernel methods.

Learning spectral features of the partial covariance operator through a bi-level contrastive objective is an interesting and potentially original synthesis. The sample-splitting design also appropriately separates representation learning from testing.

The paper attempts an unusually broad theoretical treatment, including null calibration, power, representation error, and finite-dimensional approximation. The operator-level motivation and overall testing pipeline are presented clearly.
The proposed neural feature parameterization could enable GPU-based implementations and may be practically useful if the calibration and optimization issues are resolved.
weaknesses: The central chi-squared null result is not supported by its proof. Equation (26) incorrectly infers E[uu^T⊗vv^T]=E[uu^T]⊗E[vv^T] from conditional independence given Z. Conditional independence only gives E[E[uu^T|Z]⊗E[vv^T|Z]], which generally does not factor. Consequently, even with exact residualization, the limiting covariance is generally distribution-dependent and the unstudentized statistic need not follow chi-square(d^2).

The later CLT argument has related dependence problems: the projection Q is constructed from all test-set Z values, yet the proof treats its entries as fixed coefficients when taking expectations and asserting independence. It also claims off-diagonal covariance terms vanish except for identical index pairs, overlooking shared-index and Z-dependent terms. These errors undermine Theorem 4.1 and therefore the advertised analytic p-values.

The assumptions stated in Theorem 4.1 are materially weaker than those used in its proof. The proof additionally invokes conditions such as d=o(sqrt(n)), sqrt(d)E_m→0, d^2 log(n)/n→0, and n≥cK^4d^2 log n. The treatment of learned, empirically centered features as population-centered random functions is also insufficiently justified.

The representation-error condition E_m→0 largely assumes away the main learning challenge. No consistency or rate is established for the proposed nonconvex bi-level neural algorithm, and at the null the target operator is zero, so its leading singular functions are unidentified and the spectral-gap condition discussed in Section 4 fails. Operator approximation alone also does not ensure the conditional-variance structure needed for the claimed pivotal statistic.

The learning formulation contains reproducibility-relevant inconsistencies. The main text uses w:Z→R^(2d) and a 2d-dimensional inner problem, whereas Appendix A describes w:Z→R^d and d×d matrices. Some displayed inner-loss terms are dimensionally incompatible with the main formulation. Algorithm 1 omits architectures, optimizers, batch sizes, iteration counts, regularization selection, feature dimension, and convergence diagnostics.

The experimental evidence is far too limited for the scalability, adaptivity, and validity claims. There is only one synthetic post-nonlinear benchmark, no real data, runtime or memory comparison, scaling study, ablation, sensitivity analysis, or challenging near-null alternatives. Power is essentially saturated at one, so it provides little discrimination among methods.

The reported experiment is internally inconsistent: the text says Z dimensions range from 100 to 500 and lists eight baselines, whereas the plot shows dimensions 10 to 250 and only SpecCIT, KCIT, and RCIT. The proposed method's empirical type-I error is also around 0.13–0.15 at the smallest dimension for nominal alpha=0.05, directly weakening the practical calibration claim; uncertainty intervals are absent despite only 100 repetitions.

Presentation needs substantial revision. Examples include leftover editorial text such as “(low prio),” inconsistent notation and dimensions, and an incorrect statement that the critical value satisfies P(chi-square≤c_alpha)=alpha rather than 1-alpha. There is no explicit limitations discussion, particularly concerning asymptotic-only calibration, optimization assumptions, and the observed finite-sample type-I error. The work has low direct ethical risk because the evaluation is synthetic, but computational costs and risks of using a potentially miscalibrated test in scientific or causal conclusions are not addressed.

strengths: The manuscript addresses an important problem: obtaining scalable conditional-independence tests with analytically calibrated null distributions.
The proposed connection between partial covariance operators, spectral representation learning, and an HSIC-like statistic is potentially interesting and conceptually motivated.

Sample splitting between representation learning and testing is an appropriate design choice, and the paper attempts to provide both validity and power guarantees rather than relying only on empirical performance.

The manuscript is generally organized and includes substantial proof material. weaknesses: Soundness: the central chi-squared calibration appears invalid. Equation (26) incorrectly concludes that E[u(X)u(X)^T ⊗ v(Y,Z)v(Y,Z)^T] factors into the product of the two marginal second moments using conditional independence. Conditional independence only gives E[E[uu^T|Z] ⊗ E[vv^T|Z]], which generally does not equal E[uu^T] ⊗ E[vv^T]. Consequently, the limiting covariance need not be the identity, and the unstudentized statistic need not converge to chi-squared with d^2 degrees of freedom. The same erroneous factorization recurs throughout Lemmas B.2 and B.5 and the proof of Theorem 4.1, undermining the paper's principal validity claim.

Soundness: Algorithm 1 is not dimensionally well-defined as written. The main text declares u,v in R^d, w in R^{2d}, and M in R^{d×d}, yet its empirical losses contain terms such as <w_i,Mw_j> and <u_i,Nv_j>, with N associated with the 2d-dimensional inner problem. These products are incompatible. Appendix A instead changes w and N to d dimensions, contradicting the main formulation. This prevents both implementation and verification of the claimed estimator.

Soundness: the error quantity E_m in Equation (9) bounds the approximation of the truncated operator by U_theta M_theta V_theta^*, plus whitening errors. In the power proof, however, the authors use Equation (9) as if it bounded the different residual C_UV-C_UW C_WV-[[Sigma]]_d. That implication is neither stated nor established, so Theorem 4.2 does not follow from its assumptions.

Soundness: the derivation says that a symmetrized finite-rank operator has a decomposition WNW^* with N nonnegative diagonal. A generic symmetrized operator can be indefinite. The appendix later allows a symmetric N, creating another inconsistency in the foundational bilevel construction.

Soundness and presentation: Theorem 4.1 states only sub-Gaussianity and E_m→0, while its proof invokes further dimensional-rate and conditioning requirements such as d=o(sqrt(n)), sqrt(d)E_m→0, d^2 log(n)/n→0, and bounds ensuring invertibility. The result is therefore materially stronger than what the proof attempts to establish. The null also makes the leading singular subspaces non-identifiable, an issue not treated in the consistency premise.

Significance/evidence: the experiments are far too limited to support claims of broad adaptivity or scalability. There is one synthetic family, one sample size, an extremely easy alternative on which all displayed methods attain nearly unit power, and no real-data study, runtime/memory comparison, scaling curve, ablation, or sensitivity analysis for rank, architecture, optimization, regularization, or train/test allocation.

Presentation and evidential completeness: Section 6 claims comparisons against KCIT, RCIT, Scetbon, GCIT, DGCIT, CDCIT, NNLSCIT, and CCIT, including visible drafting placeholders such as '(low prio)', but Figures 2–3 show only Ours, KCIT, and GCIT. The text says d_Z varies from 100 to 500, whereas the plots use 10 to 250. These discrepancies make the reported evaluation difficult to trust.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the paper does not provide network architectures, nonlinear functions f and g, feature dimension d, optimizer settings, learning rates, iteration counts, regularization values, data-split sizes, baseline configurations, uncertainty intervals, code, or computational resources. Even apart from the dimensional errors, Algorithm 1 leaves essential update details ambiguous.

The type-I experiment uses only 100 repetitions, yielding considerable uncertainty around a nominal 0.05 rate, but no confidence intervals are shown. It also does not test heterogeneous conditional distributions that directly expose the invalid covariance factorization behind the proposed chi-squared calibration.

Originality is moderate rather than exceptional: the main ingredients—partial covariance operators, spectral contrastive learning, sample splitting, and squared cross-covariance statistics—are inherited from existing lines of work. The bilevel combination could be novel, but its derivation and implementation are not currently sound enough to establish that contribution.

Limitations and ethics are not treated appropriately. The paper provides no dedicated limitations discussion, does not acknowledge sensitivity to learned-representation consistency, optimization failure, rank selection, or null calibration, and does not discuss misuse or uncertainty in downstream causal discovery and biomedical examples. No major intrinsic ethical hazard is evident, but the absence of such discussion is notable given the motivating applications.

Overall, these are fundamental rather than cosmetic defects: the advertised analytic null distribution is unsupported, the stated learning algorithm cannot be executed consistently from the equations, and the empirical evidence is preliminary and internally inconsistent. The paper would require a corrected statistic or studentization scheme, rebuilt proofs, a precise executable algorithm, and substantially expanded experiments before its central claims could be relied upon.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: obtaining scalable conditional-independence tests while retaining the flexibility of operator-based formulations. A reliable solution would be useful for causal discovery and related applications.
The proposed combination of partial-covariance operators, learned spectral representations, sample splitting, and an HSIC-like statistic is conceptually interesting and appears reasonably original.
The manuscript provides substantial theoretical development, including an operator-learning formulation and attempted validity and power analyses, rather than presenting only an empirical heuristic.

The high-level organization and motivation are generally clear, and the paper appropriately acknowledges the impossibility of assumption-free conditional-independence testing and describes the experiments as preliminary.
I found no material research-ethics concerns; the experiments use synthetic data and the claimed application areas do not themselves introduce immediate ethical risks.
weaknesses: The central validity result is not supported by its proof. Equation (26) factorizes E[u(X)u(X)^T tensor v(Y,Z)v(Y,Z)^T] into the product of unconditional second moments using X independent of (Y,Z) conditional on Z. Conditional independence only yields an expectation of the product of conditional second moments; it does not permit this unconditional factorization when either moment varies with Z. Since the asserted identity determines the limiting covariance and hence the chi-squared calibration, Theorem 4.1 is generally invalid without substantially stronger assumptions or studentization.

Related invalid conditional-factorization steps recur in Lemma B.2 and the subsequent CLT analysis. The proof also treats the low-rank projection correction as asymptotically negligible despite its role in canceling population dependence mediated by Z. These issues affect the paper's main claim of a universally simple chi-squared null distribution, rather than being minor proof omissions.

The proposed learning algorithm is not consistently or dimensionally defined. In the main text w has dimension 2d and M is d by d, yet the outer loss contains <w_i,Mw_j>; the inner loss similarly applies the 2d-dimensional N to d-dimensional u and v. Appendix A instead changes w to dimension d. The text also describes the symmetrization of a general finite-rank operator using a nonnegative diagonal N, although a self-adjoint symmetrization need not be positive semidefinite. These inconsistencies prevent reliable implementation and undermine the derivation.

The power theorem assumes that d captures at least half of the unknown operator's Hilbert-Schmidt energy and that the representation error E_m is small, but the paper neither proves that Algorithm 1 attains the required E_m rate nor supplies verifiable conditions under which it does. Thus the guarantees are conditional on essentially unvalidated optimization and approximation assumptions, and the choice of d depends on unknown alternative-specific spectral information.

The empirical evidence is far too limited to compensate for the theoretical problems. It consists of one synthetic model at one sample size, with no real-data or causal-discovery evaluation, no uncertainty intervals despite 100 repetitions, no sensitivity analysis, and no runtime or scaling measurements supporting the scalability claim. Power is nearly saturated for all displayed methods, making that comparison minimally informative.

The experimental reporting is internally inconsistent and insufficiently reproducible. The text says that Z ranges from dimension 100 to 500, while the plots show 10 to 250; eight baselines are announced but only KCI and GCIT appear alongside the proposed method; draft markers such as 'low prio' remain; and architecture, optimization, regularization, feature dimension, training/test split, baseline tuning, and code availability are not specified. The method also alternates between the names SCIT and SpecCIT.

Presentation is visually readable overall, but numerous notation errors, duplicated text, generic figure captions, and mismatches between theorem statements and proof-side conditions make the technical argument difficult to audit. Because the central calibration claim is unsupported and the algorithm is not presently well-defined, substantial revision is required before others can build on the contribution.

strengths: The proposed connection between partial-covariance operators, learned spectral representations, and a scalable conditional-independence statistic is original and potentially significant. The bilevel formulation is an interesting direction beyond fixed-kernel tests.

The paper is generally well organized and motivates the problem clearly. It considers diverse synthetic settings, several competitive baselines, computational cost, hyperparameter sensitivity, and a real biomedical application.

Using separate representation-training and testing samples is appropriate in principle, and the paper honestly acknowledges the absence of representation-learning rates, conservative calibration, and the difficulty of hyperparameter selection.
weaknesses: The central validity theorem is unsupported because Eq. (26) in its proof incorrectly turns conditional independence into an unconditional factorization. Under the null, the correct identity is E[E[uu^T|Z] tensor E[vv^T|Z]], which generally does not equal Cov(u) tensor Cov(v). Marginal whitening therefore does not make the asymptotic covariance identity, so the claimed chi-squared null distribution fails under ordinary conditional heteroskedasticity.

The proof contains further consequential dependence errors. The projection Q is constructed from the same test-set Z values and is consequently random and dependent on u(X) and v(Y,Z), yet subsequent covariance and Lindeberg arguments effectively treat its weights as independent or fixed. The assertion that off-diagonal covariance terms are nonzero only for identical index pairs also omits shared-index cases. These are not minor gaps because they underpin Theorem 4.1 and Type I error control.

The implemented test differs from the analyzed test in an invalid way. Appendix C performs an SVD of the observed statistic matrix, retains its largest singular components, and compares their squared norm with a chi-squared distribution whose degrees of freedom equal the retained dimension. Data-dependent selection of the largest singular values does not have that chi-squared distribution; the theorem instead concerns the full d-by-d norm with d^2 degrees of freedom. Thus the experiments do not validate the stated theory and their reported p-values are not justified.

The power result assumes that the learned representation has small approximation error and that d captures at least half of the unknown operator signal, but supplies no guarantee that Algorithm 1 achieves either property. Consequently, the theory does not establish power for the proposed training algorithm. There are also inconsistent uses of the separation parameter and several apparent algebraic/notation errors in the power proof.

The biomedical experiment violates the i.i.d. unit assumed by the test: 1,341 tile-level triplets come from only 135 whole-slide images, with patient-level molecular variables and outcomes repeated across as many as ten tiles. No patient-clustered inference or patient-level train/test split is described. This pseudoreplication can make the p-value below 0.001 and predictive accuracies severely anti-conservative, so the claimed biological conclusion is unsupported.

Experimental reproducibility is inadequate. The manuscript contains an empty code-repository entry, does not clearly report the selected hyperparameters and random seeds for each experiment, and is inconsistent about whether the new benchmark uses 500 or 5 repetitions. The tuning protocol also appears to optimize directly using simulated null and alternative performance without clearly identifying independent tuning and evaluation runs.

Presentation is polished at a high level, but important details are ambiguous or internally inconsistent, and Figure 5 is visibly clipped at the top of a page. More importantly, the generic impact statement does not address the risks of drawing clinical conclusions from clustered retrospective pathology data. Because both the theoretical calibration and the empirical testing procedure are invalid, the paper's central claim of valid conditional-independence testing is not established.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/b0d9a784c7e94f568b92c794282b9ff6/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} is motivated by an important problem and proposes an interesting connection between partial-covariance operators and learned spectral representations. The train/test split for representation learning is conceptually appropriate.

The paper is generally readable and provides substantial implementation detail, baseline comparisons, sensitivity studies, and an explicit limitations section. The authors appropriately acknowledge dependence on representation quality and the absence of a standard CI-test tuning protocol.

The empirical scope includes several nonlinear and high-dimensional synthetic settings plus a potentially useful multimodal pathology application. In some reported settings SpectralCIT is markedly better calibrated than the baselines while retaining useful power.
weaknesses: Soundness: the central chi-squared calibration theorem appears incorrect. In Appendix B.7 the proof factorizes Cov(u(X)⊗v(Y,Z)) as Cov(u(X))⊗Cov(v(Y,Z)) under X independent of Y conditional on Z. Conditional independence does not imply marginal independence because both variables can depend on Z. Likewise, the projection Q is constructed from the observed Z sample and is not independent of the feature terms, yet the covariance and Lindeberg arguments effectively treat its entries as fixed independent weights. Shared-index covariance terms claimed to vanish generally do not vanish. Marginal whitening therefore does not make the residual cross-covariance have identity asymptotic covariance, so its squared Frobenius norm need not converge to an unweighted chi-squared distribution.

The proof of Theorem 4.1 also uses material conditions absent from its statement, including d=o(sqrt(n)), n at least on the order of K^4 d^2 log n, and stronger rates involving the representation error. Thus the advertised validity result is unsupported even on its own proof's terms.

The implemented test differs from the analyzed test in a statistically consequential way. Appendix C performs an SVD of the test-statistic matrix on the test data, retains a data-dependent set of leading singular components, and compares the result with a chi-squared distribution whose degrees of freedom equal the retained rank. A truncated Frobenius norm of a d-by-d Gaussian matrix does not have chi-squared-rank calibration. No theorem or independent calibration experiment justifies this pruning procedure.

The power theorem is conditional on an unverified representation error E_m^pow and assumes d captures at least half the unknown operator energy. The paper supplies neither learning/optimization rates nor a usable method for checking these premises. Algorithm 1 uses alternating updates rather than demonstrating solution of the stated bilevel problem. Consequently, the theory does not establish power for the actual neural training procedure.

The evaluation is strongly affected by oracle-style tuning: hyperparameters are selected directly using empirical type-I error and power under the same null/alternative generators and conditioning dimensions used for benchmarking. The manuscript does not clearly identify a separate tuning benchmark or held-out repetitions. Equal tuning budgets do not remove this information advantage, and such access to labeled null and alternative distributions is unavailable in ordinary CI applications.

The breast-cancer analysis violates the i.i.d. unit assumed by the test. It converts only 135 WSIs into 1,341 tile-level triplets while repeating the patient-level molecular scores and survival outcome across as many as ten tiles. Treating tiles as independent inflates the effective sample size; a tile-level split can also leak the same patient across training and testing. Therefore the reported p-value below 0.001 and predictive improvements do not support the clinical conclusion. The boilerplate impact statement does not address this risk of overstated biomedical evidence.

Reproducibility is inadequate: the title page's code-repository field is blank, selected hyperparameter values and tuning/evaluation separation are not fully reported, and the new benchmark is said to use 500 repetitions in the text but only 5 in Figure 10's caption. The pathology annotations, patient-grouped split protocol, and predictive-model evaluation protocol are also unspecified.

The scalability claim is only weakly demonstrated: runtime is measured at the single sample size N=1000, SpectralCIT is slower than RCIT, and there is no scaling study in N, memory analysis, or accounting that makes the claimed amortization clear.

Overall, the learned-operator idea has promise, but the invalid null-distribution argument and unsupported test-time calibration undermine the paper's main claim of valid CI testing. The clinical experiment and tuning protocol do not provide an independent remedy, so substantial theoretical and empirical revision is required before the contribution can be relied upon.

strengths: Originality/significance: Learning low-rank spectral representations of the partial covariance operator through a bilevel contrastive objective is an interesting connection between classical operator-based CI testing and modern representation learning. If made valid, the train/test split and analytic chi-squared calibration could offer a useful scalable alternative to kernel or resampling tests.

Presentation: The main pipeline, test statistic, intended roles of representation error, and relationship to prior CI tests are generally explained clearly. The paper also includes extensive appendices, sensitivity analyses, runtime measurements, and several synthetic settings.

Empirical promise: SpectralCIT appears well calibrated and powerful on the reported synthetic benchmarks, including a nonsmooth setting where NNLSCIT fails. The comparison covers multiple established baselines and explores conditioning dimensions up to 300.

The limitations section appropriately acknowledges the absence of a standard tuning protocol, conservative calibration, and the lack of explicit representation-learning rates; honestly identifying these limitations is a positive feature.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central validity theorem appears unsupported. In Appendix B.4, Eq. (26) uses X independent of (Y,Z) conditional on Z to replace E[u(X)u(X)^T tensor v(Y,Z)v(Y,Z)^T] by the product of the two unconditional second moments. Conditional independence only factorizes the conditional moments; averaging their product over Z does not generally equal the product of their averages. Consequently, the claimed identity covariance and chi-squared null limit do not follow.

Theorem 4.1 assumes only sub-Gaussian learned features and E_val_m approaching zero, where E_val_m measures marginal whitening errors. Whitening alone cannot ensure valid residualization: under the null, an arbitrary orthonormal W(Z) need not make C_UV-C_UW C_WV vanish. The theorem needs an assumption controlling how well W captures the relevant conditional-expectation subspace, but no such error appears in its statement. This is a central issue because validity is the paper's primary claim.

The appendix relies on additional rate conditions, including d=o(sqrt(n)), sqrt(d)E_m approaching zero, and d^2 log(n)/n approaching zero, which are absent or insufficiently qualified in the main theorem. Several proof steps also treat matrices constructed from the same test observations as if the required independence structure were immediate, and the derivation does not clearly reconcile test-set centering with the matrix projection argument.

The power result is largely conditional on the unknown representation error E_pow_m and on choosing d large enough to capture at least half of the operator energy. No convergence result is proved for Algorithm 1, so the theory does not establish that the proposed training procedure meets either its validity or power premises. The paper's claim that its validity assumptions are weaker than regression-estimation conditions is therefore not substantiated.

Experimental evidence is vulnerable to benchmark-specific tuning. Section C selects hyperparameters using an objective that directly combines empirical Type I error and power over the same dimensions and data-generating family later used for evaluation. Even with fresh random repetitions, this uses null/alternative labels and benchmark knowledge, making the reported adaptivity and calibration less convincing without separate tuning families or fixed validation/test protocols.

Reproducibility is inadequate. The code-repository field is blank, the final selected architecture and batch-size settings are not fully reported, and important implementation details of the bilevel optimization are ambiguous—for example, Algorithm 1 says to update only w in the inner step and u,v in the outer step despite trainable M and N. The dimension-pruning procedure also appears to select singular components using the test statistic itself while changing the reference degrees of freedom, but its calibration is not theoretically justified.

The biomedical experiment treats 1,341 patches from only 135 whole-slide images as i.i.d. triplets even though patches share patient-level molecular scores and outcomes. This pseudoreplication can severely invalidate the reported p-value and may also inflate predictive accuracy if splitting occurs at patch rather than patient level. No clustered test, patient-level split, uncertainty analysis, or repeated-cohort validation is provided, so the asserted biological conclusion is not supported.

There are notable reporting inconsistencies: the new high-dimensional benchmark is described as using 500 repetitions in the appendix text but Figure 10 states five, and the very small Sachs-inspired experiment reports Type I error values of exactly zero without repetition counts or uncertainty. The impact statement also overlooks the risks of drawing clinical conclusions from a small, clustered retrospective dataset. These issues, together with the central theoretical gap, outweigh the method's promising idea and empirical results.
